text: Using Abhed. First the console, the way most people meet it. Then the command line, the way engineers and pipelines drive it. Everything you will see is a real deployment, recorded as it ran.

Sign in. Accounts are issued, never self-served, and every session belongs to one account, in one tenant. What you land on is a launchpad: the examples are drawn from the tools this deployment actually has.

Ask it something. In plan mode the agent can only read. Each tool call appears as it happens, with its arguments and its result, and a call the mode does not allow is refused and shown, not hidden. What you are watching is the audit record itself.

Now a change. In the default mode a write waits for a person: the approval card shows exactly what will be written, you approve or deny, and the decision is recorded with your name on it. Then the agent finishes the job.
Attach a document and ask about it. The file is uploaded into the session's workspace, the agent reads it inside the sandbox, and nothing about it leaves the deployment.

Every chat is replayable, step by step, from the append-only record. Search the rail, group by day, and delete a chat you no longer need. On the durable store the transcript stays for audit, marked with who deleted it.

The deployment page says what is actually in force: the model and its context window, the isolation tier, the store, the sign-in mode, whether the agent can reach the internet, and every boundary that holds, or does not.
Now the command line. The same binary, the same policy engine, the same record. Interactive when you want to steer, headless when a pipeline is driving.

Here is a headless run. Abhed dash p, a prompt, and the agent works: it globs, reads, edits, and writes. Watch the second line: the tool contract refuses a relative path and says what would have worked, and the agent recovers on its own.

Then the policy does its job. In accept-edits mode, running a command still needs approval, and with nobody there to ask, the answer is no. The agent reports what it could not do instead of pretending.
Grant exactly what the job needs: an allow rule for the test command, and nothing more. Now the suite runs, and passes. Deny rules would still hold in every mode, including bypass.

Interactive mode adds a line editor and slash commands: change the mode or the model mid-session, undo, diff, compact, fork from any earlier step, export a self-contained HTML transcript, or resume a session by id. Type while it works, and the steer lands at the next step.

For pipelines, JSON output streams one event per line. For other languages, abhed rpc is the same agent over standard input and output. And for your own Go software, the S D K gives you the loop with the same guarantees, including validated structured output.

Subagents run in parallel, each in its own git worktree. Schedules run recurring work on a clock. Skills, extensions and M C P servers extend what the agent can do without changing what it is allowed to do.
That is Abhed in use. A console for people, a command line for engineers, and one record of everything, wherever it runs.
